title: Access Questions: Building the Conditions for Universal Success in Your Tier 1 Instruction
author: The Disruptive Educator
summary: The Disruptive Educator introduces "access questions," a technique the author describes as retrieval practice meeting checking for understanding meeting David Didau's "gapless instruction," designed to solve the practical classroom problem of matching a single lesson to students with very different levels of prior knowledge. The procedure is precise: before teaching new content, identify the exact prerequisite knowledge students need, ask a short retrieval question that surfaces whether they have it, check the whole class's response, and reteach on the spot if the prerequisite genuinely isn't there, only proceeding to new content once that foundation is confirmed. The piece is grounded in the belief, quoting Siegfried Engelmann, Graham Nuthall, and David Didau, that ability is an output of instruction rather than a fixed input students arrive with, and it carefully distinguishes two different reasons an access question might reveal a gap, weak storage strength (the knowledge was never really learned, requiring reteaching) versus weak retrieval strength (the knowledge exists but is hard to access, requiring practice rather than reteaching), drawing on the New Theory of Disuse and Dylan Wiliam's related argument. The author closes by reframing the technique's stakes: while a teacher cannot undo the instructional gaps a student arrives with, treating those gaps as evidence of fixed incapacity rather than an addressable feature of prior instruction is itself a choice, and access questions are one concrete, repeatable way of acting on the alternative belief.
points: The access-question procedure is explicitly sequenced and falsifiable, identify prerequisite knowledge, ask a retrieval question, check the whole class, reteach if the gap is real, only then proceed, rather than a vague call to 'check prior knowledge' before a lesson.

The piece's distinction between storage strength (knowledge never really learned) and retrieval strength (knowledge present but hard to access), drawn from the New Theory of Disuse and Dylan Wiliam, gives teachers two genuinely different diagnoses for the same symptom (a wrong answer on an access question), each requiring a different fix, reteaching versus further retrieval practice.

Quoting three different researchers (Engelmann, Nuthall, Didau) converging on the same claim, that ability is the consequence rather than the cause of what a student knows, the piece grounds a specific classroom technique in an explicit theoretical commitment rather than presenting it as an isolated trick.

The requirement that retrieval be both 'effortful' and 'successful' (citing Hendrick and Didau) resolves an apparent contradiction in retrieval-practice advice: pure ease produces no learning benefit, but pure difficulty without success produces guessing rather than genuine reconstruction from memory, so an access question has to be calibrated, not merely hard.
quotes: Teaching only makes sense if we believe instruction changes what students know, says Caiti Wade.

Identify the prerequisite knowledge students need to access the new learning. Ask a short question that requires students to retrieve that knowledge immediately before they need it. Check the response of the whole class so you know whether students can actually access what comes next.
The curriculum will largely determine the extent to which students are smart.
Ability is the consequence, not the cause, of what children learn.

Retrieval practice works by strengthening memory traces that already exist. The act of pulling information out of long-term memory; of searching, effortfully reconstructing, generating an answer from partial cues, consolidates and stabilises what has been learned.

While I can't control the instructional gaps that have accumulated prior to students joining my class, I can control what happens in my classroom. And more to the point, I don't have to simply accept those knowledge gaps as being evidence of what a student is capable of.
